title: Deep Panda
summary: Deep Panda, tracked under names such as Shell Crew, Black Vine and KungFu Kittens, is an espionage cluster that public reporting has followed since at least 2008, with victims in government, healthcare, defence and technology. Reporting describes a strong preference for server-side entry: rather than only targeting user workstations, the operators exploit public web and application servers, then deploy web shells and built-in administration interfaces to keep access. That approach gives them a stable foothold in a network segment that is usually exposed to the internet and rarely monitored as closely as endpoints. On workstations the group has been reported using custom remote access families for document collection, and reporting has linked the cluster to high profile breaches of health insurers, although different vendors have assigned those intrusions to other names. Evidence in an environment is typically an unexpected file in a web directory, a service account running an interactive process, or outbound connections from a server that should only serve content. Attribution to a state sponsor is described in public reporting with moderate confidence and remains an assessment.

beginner.definition: Deep Panda is a name for an espionage group that has attacked governments and health companies since about 2008. Security companies also call it Black Vine or Shell Crew. The group likes to break into web servers instead of only laptops. Reports suggest a link to China, but that remains an assessment.
beginner.whyItMatters: Most teams watch user laptops closely and forget the servers that face the internet. This group lives in exactly that blind spot. A single badly protected web server can expose customer records and internal systems. If you monitor servers as carefully as laptops, this intrusion becomes much harder.
howItWorks: The attackers find a web server with out of date software or a weak administrative password.
They upload a small file, called a web shell, that runs commands through the web page.
From that server they reach internal systems, because servers are trusted by their neighbours.
They install remote control programs on some workstations to collect documents and email.
They create extra accounts and hide their files inside normal folders and services.
They keep coming back for months or years, and update their tools when defenders remove them.
beginner.example: Think of an office building where the front door is locked at night but the delivery hatch is not. A stranger climbs through the hatch, props it open with a brick, and then comes and goes whenever they want. The security guard only ever checks the front door, and the hatch looks closed from the street. By morning the brick is still there, and the hatch still opens quietly for anyone who knows about it.
takeaways: Servers that face the internet deserve the same attention as laptops.
A web shell is a file that turns a website into a command line.
Unexpected files in web directories are worth investigating immediately.

objectives: Explain how web shell persistence works on a public facing server.
Describe why a compromised server gives an attacker a trusted position.
Identify the file system and process evidence left on a compromised web server.
Explain how server-to-server trust increases the impact of one exposed host.
Describe how vendor names for one cluster can differ and overlap.
